title: Descriptive statistics: center, spread and skew
objective: Compute and interpret mean, proportion, median, mode, percentiles, range, IQR, variance, standard deviation and skew with NumPy and pandas.

items: Mean
Sum of the values divided by how many there are.
Proportion
Fraction of values with a property; the mean of a 0/1 array.
Median
Middle value of the sorted data (average of the two middle values if the count is even).
Mode
Most frequent value.
Percentile
The value with about p% of the data at or below it; quartiles are the 25th, 50th, 75th.
IQR
Q3 − Q1, the spread of the middle half; resistant to outliers.
Standard deviation
Root mean squared deviation from the mean; a typical distance from the mean.
Skew
Asymmetry: right-skewed has a long right tail and mean > median.

items.label: Standard deviation
items.note: pandas .std() divides by N−1 instead of N

blocks.md:
- **np.std vs pandas .std().** `np.std` divides by N, pandas by N − 1. A question that says "using NumPy" wants the N version.
- **Median with an even count.** Average the two middle values; don't just pick one.
- **Forgetting to sort** before finding the median or a percentile by hand.
- **Mixing up skew direction.** The skew is named after the **tail**: tail on the right, mean pulled right, mean > median.

blocks.title: Mean, variance and SD by hand, then in NumPy
blocks.problem: Five strain readings are 4, 7, 7, 10, 22. Find the mean, median, variance and standard deviation (NumPy's definition).

steps.title: Median
steps.why: Odd count: the middle value. It is below the mean because 22 pulls the mean up.

steps.title: Squared deviations
steps.why: Squares stop the deviations from cancelling.

steps.md:
```python
import numpy as np

x = np.array([4, 7, 7, 10, 22])
print("mean:", np.mean(x))
print("median:", np.median(x))
print("variance:", np.var(x))
print("SD:", round(np.std(x), 3))
```

```text
mean: 10.0
median: 7.0
variance: 39.6
SD: 6.293
```
steps.title: Complete program
steps.why: The program confirms each hand calculation.

blocks.answer: Mean 10, median 7, variance 39.6, SD ≈ 6.293. Mean > median hints at a right skew.

blocks.title: Is the pump data skewed?
blocks.problem: Using `pump_failures.csv`, report the mean, median, IQR and skew factor of `Hours`, and decide whether to describe the center with the mean or the median.

steps.title: Center
steps.why: If they differ a lot, the data are lopsided.

steps.title: Spread
steps.why: IQR isn't thrown off by the few very long-lived pumps.

steps.md: `skew()` gives the skew factor; compare with 0.5 and 1.
steps.title: Shape

steps.md:
```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

h = pd.read_csv("pump_failures.csv")["Hours"]
print("mean:", round(h.mean(), 1))
print("median:", h.median())
print("IQR:", np.percentile(h, 75) - np.percentile(h, 25))
s = h.skew()
print("skew:", round(s, 2))
if s > 1:
    print("highly right-skewed: report the median")
elif s > 0.5:
    print("moderately right-skewed: the median is safer")
else:
    print("roughly symmetric: the mean is fine")
```

```text
mean: 995.1
median: 815.0
IQR: 909.75
skew: 1.23
highly right-skewed: report the median
```
steps.title: Complete program
steps.why: The decision rule turns the skew factor into a recommendation.

blocks.answer: Mean well above median and a skew factor above 1: highly right-skewed, so the median describes a typical pump better.

blocks.title: Solution: Summarize the pump failures
blocks.md:
Full program for **Summarize the pump failures** (try it yourself first):

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

h = pd.read_csv("pump_failures.csv")["Hours"]

mean = h.mean()
median = h.median()
sd_numpy = np.std(h)
sd_pandas = h.std()
rng = h.max() - h.min()
iqr = np.percentile(h, 75) - np.percentile(h, 25)

print("mean", round(mean, 1))
print("median", round(median, 1))
print("SD numpy", round(sd_numpy, 1))
print("SD pandas", round(sd_pandas, 1))
print("range", round(rng, 1))
print("IQR", round(iqr, 1))
```

Output:

```text
mean 995.1
median 815.0
SD numpy 773.2
SD pandas 778.0
range 3409
IQR 909.8
```
